title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: All happy families are alike; each unhappy family is unhappy in its own way.

The Oblonsky household was in chaos. The wife had found out that her husband was having an affair with the French girl who had been their family's governess, and she had told him she could not go on living under the same roof with him. Three days had passed in this state, and the husband, the wife, every member of the family and every servant in the house was painfully aware of it. Everyone in the house felt that there was no point in their living together, that strangers thrown together by accident at any wayside inn had more in common with each other than they — the family and staff of the Oblonskys — had with one another. The wife stayed shut in her room; the husband had not been home for three days. The children ran wild through the house; the English governess had quarreled with the housekeeper and had written to a friend asking her to look out for a new position; the cook had walked out yesterday in the middle of dinner; the kitchen-maid and the coachman had given notice.

Three days after the quarrel, Prince Stepan Arkadyevitch Oblonsky — Stiva, as fashionable society called him — woke at his usual hour, eight in the morning, but not in his wife's bedroom: on the leather sofa in his study. He rolled his plump, well-groomed body over on the springy cushions as if he meant to slip back into a long sleep, threw his arms around the pillow on the other side and pressed his face into it; then suddenly he jumped, sat up on the sofa, and opened his eyes.

"Yes, yes, how did it go now?" he thought, going back over his dream. "How was it? Right — Alabin was giving a dinner in Darmstadt; no, not Darmstadt, somewhere American. Yes, but in the dream Darmstadt was in America. So Alabin was giving a dinner on glass tables, and the tables were singing _Il mio tesoro_ — only not exactly _Il mio tesoro_, something better — and there were these little decanters standing on the table, and the decanters were women, too," he remembered.

Stepan Arkadyevitch's eyes twinkled with amusement, and he thought it over with a smile. "Yes, it was lovely, really lovely. There was a great deal more that was charming, only you can't put it into words, or even pin it down in your thoughts once you're awake." Noticing a thin band of daylight slipping in past the edge of one of the serge curtains, he swung his feet cheerfully off the sofa and felt around for the slippers his wife had embroidered for his last birthday in gold-stitched morocco. And then, as he had done every morning for the past nine years, without getting up he reached out for the spot in his bedroom where his dressing-gown always hung. And it was at that point that he suddenly remembered he was not sleeping in his wife's room but in his study, and remembered why; the smile vanished from his face, and he frowned.

"Ugh, ugh, ugh! Oh..." he muttered, the whole quarrel rushing back. Every detail of the row with his wife came up again in his mind, the hopelessness of the situation, and — worst of all — that the fault was entirely his.

"She won't forgive me, and she can't forgive me. And the most awful part of it is that it's all my fault — all my fault, even though I'm not really to blame. That's the whole point of the situation," he reflected. "Oh, oh, oh!" he kept repeating in despair as the sharp pain of the quarrel came back over him.

The worst of it had been that first moment when he came home from the theater, happy and good-humored, with an enormous pear in his hand for his wife, and could not find her in the drawing-room, and to his surprise did not find her in his study either, and finally found her in her bedroom, holding in her hand the unlucky letter that had given everything away.

She — his Dolly, forever fussing and worrying over household details, narrow-minded, as he considered her — was sitting completely still with the letter in her hand, staring at him with an expression of horror, despair, and outrage.
"What is this? This?" she had asked, pointing at the letter.
And remembering it now, Stepan Arkadyevitch — as so often happens — was less upset by the thing itself than by the way he had handled what his wife said.

Something happened to him at that instant that happens to people when they are caught unexpectedly in something disgraceful. He could not get his face to match the position he had been put in by the discovery of his fault. Instead of being hurt, denying it, defending himself, begging forgiveness — instead even of being coolly indifferent, anything would have been better than what he did — his face, completely involuntarily (a reflex of the spinal cord, Stepan Arkadyevitch reflected, having a taste for physiology), completely involuntarily, settled into its usual good-natured and therefore idiotic smile.

That idiotic smile he could not forgive himself. When Dolly caught sight of it she shuddered as if at a stab of physical pain, broke out, with her usual fire, into a stream of cruel words, and ran out of the room. Since then she had refused to see him.
"It's that idiotic smile that's to blame for everything," Stepan Arkadyevitch thought.
"But what's to be done? What's to be done?" he kept asking himself in despair, and he could find no answer.
